prompt:
Write an explanation of about 400 words of what a leap second is and why the bodies that govern timekeeping have decided to stop adding them. The reader is a general newspaper reader.

Do not use em dashes.

text:
A leap second is a one-second adjustment added to official clocks every so often so that they stay in step with the turning of the Earth. It exists because there are two ways of measuring time, and they do not quite agree.

The first is astronomical. For most of history a day was defined by the planet's rotation: the time from one noon to the next. The second is atomic. Since 1967 the length of a second has been fixed by the vibrations of caesium atoms, which tick with extraordinary steadiness. An atomic clock would lose or gain less than a second over many millions of years.

The Earth is a far less reliable timekeeper. Its spin is slowed slightly by tides and nudged by shifts in the oceans, the atmosphere and its molten core. Over the long run, days are growing a little longer. If clocks followed only the atoms, they would slowly drift away from the Sun, and noon would eventually arrive at the wrong time of day, though only after many centuries.

To prevent this, international timekeepers created Coordinated Universal Time in 1972. It runs on atomic seconds but is kept within 0.9 of a second of the Earth's rotation. Whenever the gap threatened to exceed that, a leap second was inserted, usually at the end of June or December. A minute then contained 61 seconds, and the clock read 23:59:60 before moving into the new day. Twenty-seven have been added, the most recent at the end of 2016.

The practice was tidy for astronomers but troublesome for everyone else. Computers generally assume that every minute has 60 seconds, so an extra one can confuse software. Leap seconds have been blamed for crashes and outages at major websites, and engineers in finance, telecommunications, satellite navigation and power networks have long complained that the irregular insertion is a hazard. Some large technology companies avoid the problem by "smearing" the extra second across several hours, but each firm does it differently, which creates its own inconsistencies.

In 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures, the body that oversees the international system of units, voted to stop using leap seconds by 2035. After that date the gap between atomic time and Earth time will be allowed to grow much larger, to be dealt with at some later point, possibly by a larger correction made far less often.

Helping the decision is an odd recent trend: the Earth's rotation has been speeding up slightly, which could even call for a negative leap second, removing one. That has never been tried, and engineers fear it would be riskier still.

For ordinary people, nothing will change. Your phone will keep showing the right time. The difference is that, for the first time in decades, a second will no longer need to be argued over.
